C. FEDERAL STATUTORY PROCEDURAL 
REQUIREMENTS IN ADJUDICATION
When Congress authorizes an agency to adjudicate, what procedures 
must the agency follow? As we will see in Section D, constitutional due 
process establishes a minimum procedural “floor” for proceedings that 
involve the adjudication of protected interests in “life, liberty, or property.” 
Congress (by statute) or the agency (by regulation) may require additional 
procedures beyond the constitutional minimum. Statutory procedural 
requirements for agency adjudication are found in the APA and in each 
agency’s organic statute. When an agency’s statute requires an “on-the- 
record” hearing, the APA supplies certain minimum procedural 
requirements. Central to the APA’s hearing regime are provisions that 
empower and protect Administrative Law Judges (ALJs), the officials who 
preside over APA hearings. But the APA’s formal adjudication provisions 
apply to only a limited range of agency adjudicatory actions. Statutory 
interpretation, which is conducted in the shadow of constitutional due 
process, is thus essential for determining the procedures an agency must 
follow in adjudication.
1. WHEN IS AN APA ‘‘ON-THE-RECORD” 
HEARING REQUIRED?
Statutes provide the primary starting point for determining the nature 
and existence of hearing rights in federal programs. There are two reasons: 
First, Congress almost always provides for hearings when authorizing 
programs of adjudicatory decision making that implicate constitutionally 
protected “liberty” or “property.” Second, when Congress creates hearing 
rights, it generally prescribes their features in sufficient detail to meet any 
plausible due process minimum.
Even so, divining the existence and nature of statutory hearing rights 
turns out to be a complex enterprise, for at least four reasons.
First, although the Court interprets constitutional due process as 
guaranteeing a hearing only in adjudicatory contexts. Congress is not so 
limited. It may—and has—^prescribed hearings for rulemaking.
Second, extending the view beyond what due process requires reveals 
the existence of two broad hearing types: (1) quasi-judicial (adjudicatory); 
and (2) quasi-legislative (rulemaking). As we saw in Londoner and Bi- 
Metallic, quasi-judicial hearings are the only type of hearing that due 
process may require. Quasi-judicial hearings are trial-like or evidentiary 
hearings undertaken for the purpose of resolving fact-bound disputes. 
Although due process does not require the full trappings of the courtroom.
